Classification is now reliable, but the agent calls `classify_document` repeatedly on the same document, extractors never run, and jobs end at the iteration cap. What should you change in the loop?

options.text: Force the classifier tool on the first request only, then set `tool_choice` to `auto` so the model can pick the extractor.
options.explanation: Forcing the tool once guarantees the order. Releasing the setting afterwards lets the loop move on to extraction.

options.text: Set `tool_choice` to `any` on every request, so that the model must call a tool but may pick the classifier first.
options.explanation: `any` lets the model choose any tool, so classification might be skipped, and the loop can never end without a tool call.

options.text: Keep the forced setting and raise the iteration cap, so that the agent has enough turns to reach the extraction tools.
options.explanation: While the setting is forced, every turn calls the classifier, so extra turns can't reach an extractor.

options.text: Remove `classify_document` from the tool list and state in the system prompt that each document must be classified first.
options.explanation: The model can't call a tool that isn't listed, and a prompt doesn't guarantee the order.

questions.keyConcept: Force a specific tool only on the request where it must run, then release tool_choice for later steps.

questions.stem: The `lookup_vendor` tool returns `{"vendor": null}` both when the vendor registry times out and when a vendor is truly absent. The agent sends every null to new-vendor onboarding, and the onboarding team reports that 40% of its cases are existing vendors. Registry timeouts clear within seconds. What should `lookup_vendor` return?

options.text: An exception for both cases, so that the pipeline stops and an operator inspects each document with a missing vendor.
options.explanation: A missing vendor is a normal outcome, and timeouts clear in seconds, so neither should stop the pipeline.

options.text: `vendor: null` for both cases, plus a rule in the agent prompt to call `lookup_vendor` again before onboarding anyone.
options.explanation: The agent still can't tell the two cases apart, and every truly absent vendor now costs an extra call.

options.text: A timeout returned as the most recent cached vendor record, so that the agent can continue without any interruption.
options.explanation: Cached data presented as a fresh result hides the failure and may use out-of-date vendor details.

options.text: A timeout returned as an error with a retryable flag, and `vendor: null` only when no match exists.
options.explanation: Separating access failures from valid empty results lets the agent retry timeouts and onboard only vendors that are really absent.

questions.keyConcept: Tools must distinguish access failures from valid empty results so agents can respond correctly to each.

questions.stem: Contracts with more than 200 line items fail schema validation with `unexpected end of JSON input`. The responses show `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` and a `tool_use` block that stops partway through. Your validation retry sends the error back, but the second attempt gets cut off at about the same point. Shorter contracts extract without problems, and cost isn't a concern for this small share of documents. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Raise the `max_tokens` limit for these long contracts, and check for truncation before sending any output to validation.
options.explanation: The output was cut off by the limit, so a higher limit fixes the cause. Checking for truncation avoids pointless validation retries.

options.text: Repair the cut-off JSON in code by closing the open brackets, and save the line items that were returned.
options.explanation: This saves valid-looking JSON but silently loses every line item after the cut-off point.

options.text: Send detailed validation feedback in the retry, including the line where the JSON ended and the fields still missing.
options.explanation: The model didn't make a mistake it can correct. The retry hits the same limit however detailed the feedback is.

options.text: Make every line-item field optional in the schema, so that a partly written list can pass validation.
options.explanation: Partial contracts would pass as complete, and the missing line items would go unnoticed downstream.

questions.keyConcept: When stop_reason is max_tokens, raise the limit; validation feedback cannot fix output that was truncated.

questions.stem: Last month, 1,000 extractions failed validation. Of these, 620 had a `due_date` in the wrong format, and 380 had no `due_date` because the source document does not state one. The field is currently required, and each failure is retried up to three times with the validation error, so the 380 documents consume three extra calls and still fail. Which two changes should you make? (Select 2.)

options.text: Raise the retry limit to five attempts, so that documents with no stated date have extra chances to succeed.
options.explanation: The date isn't in the document, so further attempts can only fail or produce an invented value.

options.text: Stop retrying all 1,000 failures and send them directly to the human review queue for manual entry.
options.explanation: Most of these failures can be fixed automatically, so this spends reviewer time on work a retry would solve.

options.text: Keep retrying format failures with the specific error, because the correct date is present in the document.
options.explanation: Format errors can be corrected, because the information exists and the model only needs to know what was wrong.

options.text: Make `due_date` nullable, so a document that states no date passes validation without a retry.
options.explanation: A missing date is a valid outcome. Allowing null stops the wasted retries and stops the model being pushed to invent a date.

options.text: Set a default `due_date` of 30 days after the invoice date whenever no date can be found in the document.
options.explanation: This invents a business value that downstream systems would treat as real.

questions.keyConcept: Retry errors the model can correct, and make fields nullable when the source may not contain the value.

questions.stem: Each synchronous extraction request carries an 8,000-token system prompt of field rules, followed by the document. You add `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` at the end of the system prompt, but usage reports show almost no cache reads. The first line of the system prompt is `Processed at: ${new Date().toISOString()}`, which the audit team wants recorded with each request. Which change restores the cache reads?

options.text: Move the timestamp out of the system prompt and into the user message after the cached content, so the prefix stays identical.
options.explanation: Caching needs an identical prefix. A timestamp at the start changes the prefix on every request, so moving it after the cached content allows reuse.

options.text: Add the `"ttl": "1h"` option to the `cache_control` block, so that cached entries last long enough to be reused.
options.explanation: A longer lifetime doesn't help, because the changing timestamp means no two requests share a prefix.

options.text: Round the timestamp to the nearest minute, so that requests sent within the same minute can share one cached prefix.
options.explanation: This allows only brief reuse and makes the audit timestamp less accurate, while moving the value fixes the problem fully.

options.text: Add `cache_control` breakpoints to each document as well, so that a larger part of every request is eligible for caching.
options.explanation: Each document is different and comes after the changing prefix, so extra breakpoints produce no cache hits.

questions.keyConcept: Prompt caching needs an identical prefix, so changing values such as timestamps must come after the cached content.

questions.stem: The extraction prompt has four few-shot examples. Two show dates as `2024-03-01` and two show them as `March 1, 2024`, because they were copied from different projects. The output now mixes both formats, and roughly half of the records need fixing downstream. The examples are otherwise accurate and cover the layouts that matter. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Remove all four examples, so that the model falls back on the format described in the schema.
options.explanation: The examples cover important layouts, so removing them gives up accuracy to fix a formatting issue.

options.text: Rewrite all four examples to show dates in the one format that downstream systems expect.
options.explanation: The model is copying the inconsistent examples. Making them consistent fixes the cause and keeps their coverage of the layouts.

options.text: Convert the dates in code after extraction by trying both formats, and keep the examples unchanged for now.
options.explanation: Downstream conversion hides the inconsistency, and ambiguous dates can be converted incorrectly.

options.text: Add a fifth example showing the preferred format, and leave the existing four examples as they are.
options.explanation: The conflicting examples would remain, so the model would still see both formats.

questions.keyConcept: Few-shot examples set the output format, so every example must show the same format the system expects.

questions.stem: A schema field `currency` is an enum of ISO codes. Some invoices show only `$`, and the supplier could be in the US, Canada or Australia. The model usually picks `USD`, and finance found about 200 misposted Canadian invoices last quarter. Reviewers can settle these cases quickly when they can see what the invoice shows. Which two changes handle these invoices correctly? (Select 2.)

options.text: Remove the enum, so that `currency` can hold whatever text the model reads from the invoice.
options.explanation: Downstream systems need consistent codes, and free text doesn't resolve the ambiguity.

options.text: Set `temperature` to 0, so that the model returns the same currency value for similar invoices.
options.explanation: The model would give the same wrong answer more consistently, because the schema still has no way to express uncertainty.

options.text: Add an `"unclear"` enum value with a `currency_detail` field that records what the invoice actually shows.
options.explanation: The schema then has an honest answer for ambiguous invoices, and the detail field gives reviewers what they need.

options.text: Default `currency` to `USD` when only a symbol appears, because most suppliers in the system are American.
options.explanation: This makes the current mistake official and would keep misposting Canadian and Australian invoices.

options.text: Add to the prompt a rule for when to choose `"unclear"`, with an example of a bare `$` and no other evidence of the country.
options.explanation: The model needs a clear rule and an example, otherwise it will keep defaulting to the most common currency.

questions.keyConcept: Give enums an unclear value with a detail field, and tell the model when to use it.

questions.stem: The extractor emits field-level confidence that has been calibrated on a labelled set. Each day about 900 documents are flagged for review, and reviewers can handle 400. Items are reviewed in arrival order, so high-risk documents often wait for days. Flagged documents with conflicting values between pages have the highest error rate. Hiring isn't an option this year. Which change makes the best use of reviewer time?

options.text: Keep arrival order, but ask reviewers to spend less time on each document so that the daily count goes up.
options.explanation: Rushed reviews lower quality, and high-risk documents would still wait behind low-risk ones.

options.text: Order the queue so documents with contradictions and the lowest calibrated confidence are reviewed first.
options.explanation: With limited capacity, the riskiest documents should get human attention first, and the calibrated scores make that ordering meaningful.

options.text: Review a random sample of 400 flagged documents each day and auto-approve the remaining 500.
options.explanation: Flagged documents need review, and random selection could approve the riskiest ones without a check.

options.text: Lower the confidence threshold until only 400 documents a day are flagged, which matches what reviewers can handle.
options.explanation: Setting the threshold by staff capacity auto-approves documents that the calibration says are risky.

questions.keyConcept: When review capacity is limited, prioritise contradictory and lowest-confidence documents rather than arrival order.

questions.stem: A contract agent processes 300-page agreements over many turns and summarises earlier turns to save context. After summarisation, the liability cap of $2,500,000 is recorded as "a multi-million cap", and the renewal date disappears. Extraction later needs these exact values. The agent must stay within its context budget. How should the agent keep these values?

options.text: Stop summarising and keep the full history of every turn, so that the exact values remain available.
options.explanation: A 300-page agreement over many turns won't fit within the context budget without summarising.

options.text: Keep exact values such as amounts and dates in a persistent facts block that summarisation never touches.
options.explanation: A separate facts block preserves exact values at a small context cost, while the rest of the history can still be summarised.

options.text: Ask the summariser in its prompt to try harder to preserve every important detail from earlier turns.
options.explanation: Summaries compress by nature, so a request to try harder can't guarantee that exact values survive.

options.text: Summarise at shorter intervals, so that each summary covers fewer turns and loses fewer details at a time.
options.explanation: Frequent summaries repeat the compression, so details can be lost sooner rather than later.

questions.keyConcept: Store exact transactional facts in a persistent block outside summarised conversation history.

questions.stem: Reviewers checking extracted contract fields have to search each 80-page document to find where a value came from. The schema stores only the value, such as `"notice_period": "90 days"`, and audits need proof of each value's origin. What should the schema add for each extracted field?

options.text: A confidence score, so that reviewers know how much to trust the value.
options.explanation: A score suggests how much to trust a value, but it doesn't show where the value came from.

options.text: The source page number and the exact excerpt that the value was taken from.
options.explanation: A page number and excerpt let a reviewer or auditor confirm each value directly against the source.

options.text: A model-written explanation of why this value is the correct one to use.
options.explanation: The model's own justification isn't proof. Auditors need to see the source text.

options.text: The document title and the date on which the extraction was processed.
options.explanation: This identifies the document, which reviewers already know, but not the location of the value within it.

questions.keyConcept: Store a source page and excerpt with each extracted field so that values can be traced and audited.

questions.stem: The `match_vendor` step compares each invoice with the vendor master. For one invoice it returns `Acme Industrial GmbH` at 0.91 and `Acme Industries GmbH` at 0.90, with different bank details. The job runs unattended in a nightly batch, so nobody can answer a question during the run. Posting to the wrong vendor would send a payment to the wrong account. What should the pipeline do?

options.text: Hold this single invoice for human review with both candidates and their scores, and post the rest of the batch as normal.
options.explanation: The match is ambiguous and a mistake is costly, so a person should decide. The rest of the batch can carry on.

options.text: Fail the whole nightly batch so that an operator can resolve the ambiguity before any invoices are posted.
options.explanation: One ambiguous invoice shouldn't stop all the others from being processed.

options.text: Post to `Acme Industrial GmbH`, because it has the higher score and both scores are above the 0.85 match threshold.
options.explanation: A 0.01 difference doesn't identify the right vendor, and the cost of being wrong is a misdirected payment.

options.text: Ask the model to pick the better candidate with a one-sentence reason and then post the invoice to that vendor.
options.explanation: A confident explanation doesn't resolve the ambiguity, and the payment would still go out without a human check.

questions.keyConcept: Route ambiguous high-risk matches to human review with the candidates, instead of guessing or failing the whole batch.

questions.stem: OCR fails on pages 41–46 of an 80-page contract, and the pipeline continues with the remaining pages. The extraction then reports `termination_clause: null`, which downstream systems read as "this contract has no termination clause". Legal found two such contracts last quarter, and both clauses were on unread pages. Most documents have no OCR failures. Which two changes stop unread pages being read as missing clauses? (Select 2.)

options.text: Stop processing any contract as soon as one page fails, and discard the values already extracted from its other pages.
options.explanation: This throws away valid results from the pages that were read, when only the coverage gap needs handling.

options.text: Have the model infer the likely termination clause from the pages it could read, and fill in the field.
options.explanation: This invents legal content for pages nobody has read.

options.text: Make `termination_clause` a required non-null string, so that the model has to find a value in every contract.
options.explanation: Some contracts really have no such clause, and requiring a value pushes the model to invent one.

options.text: Record which pages could not be read in the output, so that a null can be told apart from an absent clause.
options.explanation: Coverage information shows downstream systems that the value is unknown, not that the clause is absent.

options.text: Send documents with unread pages to human review instead of passing their null values on as final results.
options.explanation: A person can check the unread pages, so a missing clause isn't treated as a confirmed absence.

questions.keyConcept: Report partial coverage explicitly so downstream systems can tell unread content apart from content that is absent.
